(AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell) (Rebecca Blackwell/AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell) By DAVID FISCHER, Associated Press July 27, 2026 at 3:39 pm EDT MIAMI — Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said Monday. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for Aug. 13 to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. The brothers weren't in court Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest . The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Attorneys for the brothers said Monday that they want the U.S. government to turn over documents that U.K. officials submitted to secure their arrest. “They don't have anything but the accusations,” attorney Joseph McBride said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.” The U.K. has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the State Department, Assistant U.S. Attorney Alejandra López said in court. The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation. “For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They've traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.” The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn't expect any help from the president. McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that "they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit," he said. McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn't gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. https://euobserver.com/232726/russia-is-.text: Every day, the Ukraine Battlefield update newsletter offers a clear look at how the war is unfolding on the ground. Subscribe for free here to get the full text delivered to your inbox. There are growing numbers of jet-powered Shaheds, and they are far more dangerous. Why they are difficult to intercept. Without Western components and Chinese engines, Russia would not have been able to build them. A jet-powered “drone-missile” also crashed in Moldova. The British crossed another red line and angered the Kremlin. Photo and map of the day: destroyed Kupiansk. Videos of the day: capture of 30 Russian soldiers; a harsh summer in the Odesa region. There are growing numbers of them, they are far more dangerous, and much more difficult to neutralise. Although Russian ballistic-missile attacks are currently causing Ukrainians the greatest concern, as they face a critical shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles and the situation is expected to deteriorate significantly by winter, attack drones remain Russia’s most widely used weapon against Ukrainian cities. However, since Ukrainians have significantly improved their air defences with their own interceptor drones and have increasingly struck deep inside Russian territory, Russia has also been deploying growing numbers of new ‘Shahed’ drone variants, called Geran-4 and Geran-5. They are far more difficult to neutralise and cause even greater damage and civilian tragedies. One of the most thoroughly documented uses of a Geran-4 was the attack on a supermarket in Chernihiv on 27 July, which killed two people — including a nine-year-old girl — and injured another 25. The drone was fitted with a camera, so the attackers probably struck the shop deliberately. Ukrainian intelligence linked the attack to a specific unit from the third combat group of the GROM “Cascade” separate unmanned systems brigade. The jet-powered drone was launched by “privileged individuals” from the Bryansk region. According to HUR , these are officers, lawyers, officials and regional commanders who terrorise Ukrainian civilians under short-term contracts, thereby gaining war-veteran status without risking deployment to combat zones. Another dangerous Russian innovation in drone warfare is the hybrid Banderol, which apparently crashed in Moldova this week and which we examine in more detail below. Ukrainian air force radars can distinguish jet-powered drones more easily from older types because they are faster. Instead of propellers, they have jet engines and their design resembles that of conventional guided missiles, but at a far lower production cost. The approach of jet-powered Shaheds towards Ukrainian cities is also evident from the air force’s increasingly frequent social-media warnings flagging the new variant: Ukrainian military experts now speak of a new phase in the air war. Mykhailo Fedorov, the recently dismissed Ukrainian defence minister, has even referred to a change in military strategy in the air. “Our response must be swift if we are to continue defeating Russia in every technological cycle,” he wrote on Telegram. “Shaheds remain the primary instrument of Russian terror, and their share is far higher than that of missiles. We can shoot them down, but they pose a problem both in terms of numbers and technological development,” Odesa-based military expert Oleksandr Kovalenko also told us. According to him, Russia can produce around 130 to 140 jet-powered drones a day. According to the Militarnyi website , the figure could be as much as twice that. “They have constantly modified them, changing their navigation and fuel systems. They have even repeatedly changed the material used in their production, although the overall architecture has not fundamentally changed. It is still a flying wing, but the material from which it is made changes,” Kovalenko, the Ukrainian expert, explained, adding that Russia makes the drones lighter or more robust depending on its needs. The two main types Russia uses are the Geran-2, an analogue of Iran’s Model 136, and an analogue of Model 238, the jet-powered version. The new Geran-5, introduced in 2026, has a range of around 950 km and, according to HUR, carries a 90-kg explosive payload. By comparison, the first Shaheds carried 20-kg warheads. Russia is seeking to expand the production of jet-powered drones, which Kovalenko currently estimates account for around 20 to 25 percent of all variants of these kamikaze drones. According to Ukrainian air force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat , jet-powered drones accounted for as much as two-thirds of the total in some attacks. “It appears that the Russian command has chosen this as its main task and the key direction for drone development,” Kovalenko said. Why they are difficult to intercept. Kovalenko also said that jet-powered Shahed variants had recently become the main challenge for Ukraine’s short-range air defence. The main reason is that they can reach speeds of up to 600 km/h. Wild Hornets units, for example, showed what the destruction of a Russian jet-powered drone looks like . Soldiers from Ukraine’s 81st Air Assault Brigade showed the same. “When they fly at maximum speed, it is relatively difficult to intercept them using standard anti-aircraft, or interceptor, drones. The drone operator has to wait until the Shahed starts manoeuvring. It slows down while manoeuvring, which makes it possible to intercept it at that point. When they are approaching their target, they reduce their speed and become more vulnerable,” Kovalenko said. As he added, the difficulty is that interceptor drones can neutralise them only by waiting for a specific and rare moment. Anton Zemlianyi, an analyst at Ukraine’s Centre for Security and Cooperation, made a similar point to RBC-Ukraine . However, he warned that Russia’s arms industry cannot manufacture jet-powered drones on the same mass scale as older variants. They are more technically complex, while their components are less readily available and more expensive. He cited the more demanding manufacture of jet engines in particular, a problem Russia addresses mainly through imports from China. According to Zemlianyi, the composite materials from which the drones themselves are made are another challenge. He described jet-powered drones as an intermediate category — between conventional long-range drones and cruise missiles. Ukraine is seeking to respond to the new challenges by developing its own jet-powered interceptor drones with similar speeds, which, according to former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov , are currently undergoing combat testing. According to him, Ukraine has one of the world’s most advanced “small-scale” air-defence systems, from which other armies are also drawing lessons. “The task now is to make ten times the effort to counter the threat of jet-powered drones as quickly as possible,” Fedorov added. It would not be possible without Western components. When Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) analysed downed Geran-4 drones — and the same applies to the Geran-5 — it found dozens of foreign components, according to a published 3D model . For example, China supplies engines disguised as industrial cooling units in order to circumvent Western sanctions. In the case of the Geran-5, HUR found at least nine US electronic components and a German transistor, in addition to Chinese components. These were not old stockpiles but new devices, showing that Russia has been successful in circumventing Western sanctions. “When it comes to the range of Western components, Russia remains dependent on smuggling, predominantly via China,” Kovalenko said. This particularly concerns microchips and microcircuits. If Russia did not have access to these technologies, it would lack the capacity to manufacture these Shaheds, which only confirms the importance of tightening the sanctions regime against Russia. Banderol crashed in Moldova. Another example of a Russian jet-powered drone is the S8000 Banderol, which some describe as a cruise missile. It is a hybrid of a cruise missile and a drone, developed by the Russian company Kronstadt. It was apparently this Russian weapon that crashed in a field in Moldova earlier this week, where Russia controls the unrecognised republic of Transnistria and has so far unsuccessfully sought to reverse the pro-European course of this small country between Romania and Ukraine. Moldovan police footage. According to the Moldovan police, fragments of a jet engine were found near the crater. This is already the second similar incident this month. In protest, Moldovan diplomacy recalled its ambassador from Moscow for consultations after the first incident. Ukrainian intelligence had previously identified components from around 30 foreign companies — from China, Japan and the US to South Korea — in a Banderol following a Russian attack. Russia also used this weapon to attack Kyiv on 2 July, killing 30 people. This drone-missile can fly at speeds of around 600 km/h and carries an even heavier warhead than the Geran-5. Notably, it does not launch directly from the ground; it is primarily carried by Russia’s Kronstadt Orion reconnaissance and strike drone. In the future, Russia would also like to integrate it with Mi-28N helicopters. According to Moldovan president Maia Sandu , such incidents occur deliberately on Moldovan territory so that Russia can test its ability to respond. According to the Institute for the Study of War, the Kremlin is demonstrating a willingness to risk its weapons striking countries neighbouring Ukraine. Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation counted at least 12 probably Russian drones and missiles that entered European airspace between 15 July and 15 August. Infographic — Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation According to ISW , this is part of Russia’s “Phase Zero” campaign, intended to create the informational and psychological conditions for potential future provocations against Nato. “This also includes Russian false-flag provocations, drone incursions, sabotage, electronic warfare jamming and overflights,” the US think-tank added. The British crossed a Kremlin red line. We have regularly reported in the Ukraine Battlefield update on how Ukrainians have fundamentally changed the dynamics of the war with their own jet-powered drones and missiles, which they use to strike major warehouses, refineries and arms complexes. It is estimated that attacks on Wildberries alone caused damage of up to 878bn roubles over two months, which, according to Vazhnyye Istorii , is comparable to the revenue that oil and gas brought to the Russian budget in April, when prices were driven up by the Israeli-American war against Iran. In recent days, however, reports have caused a stir that Ukrainians are also using the British jet-powered Nyan drone, made by Callen-Lenz, a subsidiary of arms giant BAE Systems, for strikes deep inside Russian territory, as well as another unnamed, longer-range type that is also of British origin. The Times reported this , for example, while aviation expert Valerii Romanenko confirmed it to NV . He said they had targeted, for instance, refineries in Volgograd and Yaroslavl, as well as the aforementioned Wildberries warehouses. Their range is up to 250 km, and up to 960 km in the case of the second drone. They are similar in size to Russian Shaheds, but have a much lighter warhead than the most advanced Geran variants. Until recently, London officially supplied Kyiv only with Storm Shadow guided missiles, which are highly effective but cost more than £750,000 each to manufacture — roughly 10 times more than the new drones mentioned above. The current British approach is another indication of how profoundly the nature of drone warfare has changed. London has also crossed another unwritten red line set by Moscow. By the end of the year, it is due to supply Ukraine with 160,000 drones of various types. The Kremlin responded to the reports as expected, accusing London of deliberately escalating the Ukrainian crisis and describing it as an accomplice to bloody crimes. But the UK ministry of defence told the BBC that it stood alongside Ukraine. “Russia should be in no doubt about this government’s resolve to confront Russian aggression in Ukraine, as well as against the United Kingdom and our allies,” the UK ministry said, adding that it was prepared to provide Ukraine with the equipment it needed to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion. Photo and map of the day Destroyed Kupiansk. The list of towns in eastern Ukraine completely destroyed during Russia’s invasion is very long. This is how operators of unmanned systems from the 41st Separate Mechanised Brigade see Kupiansk, on the banks of the Oskil river in the Kharkiv region. “Life once thrived on these streets, filled with children’s laughter and the bustle of adults — until the horde came and turned this picturesque, welcoming town into a nest of death and darkness,” they wrote in a post about the town, where the situation has again become very tense this summer and Russian forces are intensifying their attacks. Illustration — DeepState Videos of the day Liberation of the village of Andriivka-Klevtsove. A video by the third regiment shows the course of an operation on the Oleksandrivka axis in the Donetsk region, near the border with the Dnipropetrovsk region, during which 30 Russian soldiers were captured. This was estimated to be around half of the deployed force. The village was formerly called Iskra; it was renamed after the adoption of the so-called decommunisation law. We reported yesterday in the Ukraine Battlefield update on the successful Ukrainian operation in this part of the front. Since the start of the year, Ukrainians have retaken 745 square kms and 26 villages across the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk regions. Russia currently holds positions in the Dnipropetrovsk region only near the village of Dachne. The liberation of the village of Andriivka-Klevtsove (formerly known as Iskra) by soldiers of the 3rd Regiment and one of the Psychological Operations Centers of Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces. During the operation, 30 Russian servicemen — roughly half of the Russian… pic.twitter.com/9s9KDbNDIX — Yigal Levin (@YigalLevin) August 17, 2026 Harsh swimming in the Odesa region. Russia is responding to Ukrainian strikes with heavy attacks on Ukrainian ports in the Odesa region. This video shows, for example, what summer 2026 looks like on the beach in the village of Prymorske. What are the losses No changes on Tuesday morning. By Monday (17 August), Russia had verifiably lost 24,005 pieces of heavy equipment (23,982 on Monday, 10 August). Of these, 18,977 (18,957) were destroyed by Ukraine, 997 (995) were damaged, 1,193 (1,193) were abandoned by their crews, and 2,838 (2,837) were captured by the Ukrainian army. This includes 4,437 (4,437) tanks, of which 3,343 (3,343) were destroyed in combat. Ukraine had lost 11,916 (11,828) pieces of equipment, of which 9,333 (9,286) were destroyed, 695 (695) damaged, 692 (691) abandoned and 1,196 (1,196) captured. This includes 1,450 (1,450) tanks, of which 1,111 (1,111) were destroyed in combat. Note: Neither side regularly reports its own dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project , which has compiled a list of equipment losses documented exclusively by photographs since the beginning of the war. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/30/nort.text: The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un rejected on Wednesday South Korean findings that the North planted land mines that injured three South Korean soldiers last week and threatened to retaliate if the South fires on North Korean troops fortifying the border.The incident could further inflame tensions between the two Koreas, which have no working military hotlines or other emergency communications channels as Pyongyang hardens its stance towards Seoul while expanding its military nuclear programme.Three South Korean soldiers were injured in two explosions on 21 September near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the heavily fortified border buffer zone between the two sides.The statement by Kim Yo-jong came after South Korea’s military announced a preliminary assessment on Monday that the blasts were caused by North Korean mines following a joint inspection of the site with the US-led United Nations Command.Kim calls Seoul's claims a 'farce'Kim Yo-jong, who is considered the second most powerful figure in Pyongyang, called the South Korean assessment a “conspiratorial farce,” accusing Seoul of making groundless claims to create a pretext for provocation against the North.North Korea in recent years has added mines, anti-tank barriers and other front-line fortifications, raising concerns in the South about the growing presence of North Korean soldiers near the border.Kim criticised the South for broadcasting warnings and firing warning shots at North Korean troops conducting front-line fortification work, insisting “our soldiers have never crossed the border.”“If the (South Korean) military gangsters fire at our soldiers carrying on the permanent project for the southern border, not warning shots, our border units will take immediate and merciless retaliatory action,” she said.The recent explosions, which took place about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line, came during an operation to establish a patrol route through a densely vegetated area.The route was intended to allow future inspections with the UN Command after South Korea since last year detected “terrain changes” that may have resulted from North Korean minelaying.The DMZ is a 248-kilometre strip and one of the world’s most heavily fortified borders, with an estimated 2 million land mines, barbed-wire fences, tank traps and combat troops on both sides.In August 2015, another spate of land mine blasts that maimed two South Korean soldiers and sharply raised tensions between the Koreas.The Koreas then traded threats, staged weapons demonstrations and resumed border propaganda broadcasts before days of marathon talks eventually pulled them back from the brink.North Korea issued a vague expression of regret over the soldiers’ injuries at the time but has never clearly accepted responsibility.UN Command says North Korea violated armistice agreementThe UN Command said on Wednesday that North Korea had violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War.The agreement prohibits both sides from committing any hostile act “within, from, or against” the DMZ and bans military or civilian personnel from crossing the military demarcation line without authorisation from the armistice commission.The UN Command said it was addressing the violation through established mechanisms but didn’t elaborate.Kang Hyunwoo, the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff’s director of operations, said the military “strongly urges” North Korea to apologise for the blasts and take “responsible measures” to prevent a recurrence.South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the South would consider unspecified “corresponding measures” if a complete investigation confirms the North was responsible.

https://www.irishtimes.com/world/europe/.text: Europe Europe Letter How worried should we be about a Russian military attack? Many analysts believe a campaign of hybrid interference and sabotage in Europe will continue Jack Power Thu Sept 24 2026 - 06:00 • 4 MIN READ A police investigator at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 5th after airport workers discovered a drone equipped with explosives. Photograph: Jens Schlueter/Getty Images T he Baltic countries spent years warning western European governments about underestimating the threat Russia posed to the east. Ironically, after being proved right by the invasion of Ukraine , the Baltic trio – Estonia , Latvia and Lithuania – now have to tamp down alarm about Moscow mulling a military attack on an EU state. It is understandable that public anxieties are on edge. The discovery of a drone carrying explosives in Leipzig airport last month appeared to represent a fresh escalation in Moscow’s “hybrid war”. The German government took the unusual step of directly attributing the attempted attack to Russia, which Moscow denied. A well-documented trail of arson attacks, sabotage, rogue drone disruptions and other suspicious incidents on European soil point back towards Russia. It would seem the modus operandi is to spread fear while maintaining plausible deniability. READ MORE Welcome to the new Global Briefing newsletter ‘We don’t talk about it much’: Three years after October 7th attacks, Emily Hand is rebuilding her childhood Europe wants to get tough on China. The risks could be enormous Flydubai hijacking attempt could aid Netanyahu’s re-election bid What about an actual military attack? Russia’s FSB security services instituted a temporary curfew in two districts near the Estonian border, beside Narva, in recent days. That naturally led online commentators to ask what was going on. CIA director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Moscow a couple of weeks ago followed a US intelligence assessment – details reported by the Wall Street Journal – speculating that Russian president Vladimir Putin might try to test Nato resolve in the next few years. And last week Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk told parliament Russia could fire missiles or drones at European targets near Ukrainian territory and then claim the attacks were accidental. But the prospect of Russian tanks and troops streaming across into Narva, Vilnius or Poland, even as part of some limited incursion, is extremely low – for the foreseeable future anyway. Latvia’s national security bureau, SAB, released a statement assuring people “the likelihood of a conventional attack on the Baltic States and Nato is currently and in the near future very low”. Russia’s army is tied up in Ukraine, suffering steep casualties for small, grinding gains in the eastern Donbas region. Putin may announce a mobilisation to draft recruits this autumn and replenish military ranks. There is no known intelligence to suggest Moscow is preparing to open a second front in the war. Russian troop levels near the EU’s eastern border may be at their lowest ever because so many are fighting in Ukraine. “They haven’t got the numbers,” said John Foreman, a former UK government defence attache who was posted to Moscow from 2019 to 2022, the year of the full-scale invasion. “This is not 2022. There are no significant Russian troops anywhere near the border. [ The Estonian city that fears it’s next on Putin’s list Opens in new window ] “All this war talk is a big distraction. In 2022 people didn’t want to believe there would be an invasion, now the confirmation bias is going the other way,” he said. The more immediate danger, Foreman argues, is Russia’s ability to exploit divisions within Europe through sabotage, disinformation and political interference. Foreman said Russia would need 10 years to fully reconstitute its army and economy after the Ukraine war ends and would have to garrison large numbers of troops across occupied land it captured in the Donbas in any truce scenario as well. That’s no reason to be complacent. For Irish people, the danger feels very far removed. But other European countries, particularly those neighbouring Russia and its ally Belarus, are spending vast sums to rearm their militaries and stiffen defences to deter Putin. The invasion of Ukraine should not have caught anyone by surprise. The UK and US governments were sounding the alarm about a troop build-up, privately and publicly, for months before February 2022, warning Putin was plotting an invasion. “We had incredible intelligence ... Something’s up lads,” Foreman recalled. Paris, Berlin and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy were reluctant to heed those warnings. “They didn’t keep their minds open,” said Foreman. [ Russian actions ‘reckless and dangerous’ says EU after Baltic security incidents Opens in new window ] Senior sources in the Estonian government are confident their intelligence networks have a very accurate read on what’s going on across their border. If there is cause for concern the Baltic countries will be shouting from the rooftops. The chance of a future Russian military attack on an EU state would increase significantly if Ukraine’s defences collapsed and Russia won the war outright. The Kremlin has a high tolerance for risk. Putin gambled Russian forces would steamroll Ukraine in a couple of weeks. His so-called special military operation turned into a deadlocked 4½-year war that doesn’t look like it will end any time soon. The campaign of hybrid interference and sabotage in Europe will continue, pitched below the level triggering Nato’s article five, the common defence clause of the western military alliance. It is easy to imagine Russia making a grave miscalculation when operating inside this “grey zone”. Perhaps a bomb intended to damage infrastructure instead kills multiple civilians in Warsaw, Tallinn or Madrid, necessitating a forceful European response. That would pull everyone into uncharted territory.
